content: The primary use of molecular WHO-recommended rapid diagnostic tests (mWRDs) should be as an initial diagnostic tool for tuberculosis (TB) and drug-resistant TB (DR-TB). It is important not to confuse their diagnostic role with their potential use in screening. Priority should be given to ensuring universal access to mWRDs for diagnostic purposes before considering their use in screening programs. Expanding their use for screening would have significant financial and operational implications, which must be carefully evaluated. When mWRDs are used in a screening context rather than for diagnosis, the pretest probability of TB becomes a critical factor in deciding whether to repeat the test or proceed with treatment. Due to the high specificity of mWRDs (99%), a positive result is likely to be a true positive when the pretest probability is high. For people living with HIV (PLHIV) who are hospitalized and in settings where TB prevalence is at least 10%, a positive mWRD result should prompt consideration of treatment if the clinical presentation aligns with TB. However, the detection of TB DNA does not always indicate active TB, particularly in patients with a history of TB treatment within the past five years. This is especially true for highly sensitive molecular tests like Xpert Ultra, where culture testing can help clarify the results. In hospitalized PLHIV, co-infections are common, and a thorough investigation should be conducted. In settings with a low pretest probability of TB, despite the high specificity of mWRDs, more than half of positive results may be false positives. In such cases, repeating the mWRD test is warranted, but this should be guided by clinical evaluation and additional investigations. Treatment decisions should be based on the totality of clinical and diagnostic evidence. The diagnostic algorithms for TB have evolved significantly, with the number of recommended tests increasing from five to nine, including moderate-complexity automated nucleic acid amplification tests (NAATs). This represents a major improvement over the past when smear microscopy was the only option. Countries now have the flexibility to choose diagnostic tools that best suit their needs, with the ultimate goal of meeting patient requirements. Initial test options include those that detect TB only (e.g., TB-LAMP) and those that also detect rifampicin (RIF) resistance, either simultaneously or in a two-step process (e.g., Xpert MTB/RIF, Xpert Ultra, Truenat MTB, Truenat MTB Plus, Truenat MTB-RIF Dx, and moderate-complexity automated NAATs). Detecting RIF resistance is essential to achieving universal drug susceptibility testing (DST). Among tests that detect RIF resistance, some provide this information in a two-step process, separating TB detection from RIF resistance testing. This second step can be used as a follow-up test for initial tests that do not offer RIF resistance detection. The complexity of test procedures varies, with some tests requiring basic pipetting skills and being suitable for decentralization, while others, such as moderate-complexity automated NAATs, require more infrastructure but offer higher throughput and additional resistance detection (e.g., isoniazid [INH] resistance). In practice, the choice of diagnostic tests and algorithms will depend on the specific setting within a country or region. Hybrid models that combine tests from different manufacturers may provide a safety mechanism in case of supply chain issues. Algorithm 1 is the preferred starting point for most patients, supporting the diagnosis of pulmonary and extrapulmonary TB and achieving universal DST. It is designed to be used with any mWRD for detecting Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex (MTBC), although minor modifications may be needed depending on the test and population. Algorithm 2 may be more appropriate for certain patients, such as PLHIV, who would benefit from rapid point-of-care testing. Testing using Algorithms 1 and 2 in parallel is recommended. Algorithms 3 and 4 follow Algorithm 1, with the split based on RIF resistance results. Algorithm 3 focuses on patients with confirmed RIF-resistant TB (RR-TB) and aims to provide additional rapid DST, while Algorithm 4 addresses RIF-susceptible TB and aims to detect INH resistance or fluoroquinolone (FQ) resistance in cases of INH-resistant TB (Hr-TB). Rapid early diagnosis of FQ resistance among multidrug-resistant TB (MDR-TB) or RR-TB patients is critical, and low-complexity automated NAATs are preferred for scaling up and increasing access. A new molecular test for pyrazinamide (PZA) resistance is recommended for use on isolates at higher levels of the laboratory network for selected patients. An interlinked laboratory network offering a range of tests may best meet patient needs. The adoption of moderate-complexity automated NAATs as initial diagnostic tests that also detect INH resistance will increase the detection of Hr-TB, which has a higher incidence than RR-TB. Patients with Hr-TB require treatment regimens that include FQs. For patients diagnosed using moderate-complexity automated NAATs that detect both RIF and INH resistance, options for FQ resistance detection include low-complexity automated NAATs or line-probe assays (LPAs). In settings with a high burden of Hr-TB, follow-up testing with low-complexity automated NAATs is simpler and more cost-effective than performing both first-line and second-line LPAs. Algorithm 1 is the preferred diagnostic pathway for individuals being evaluated for pulmonary and extrapulmonary TB, as well as for achieving universal DST. It aligns with the goals of the End TB Strategy and is designed to be used with any mWRD for MTBC detection. In settings with a reliable referral system and a high risk of Hr-TB, moderate-complexity automated NAATs may be preferred as the initial test due to their ability to simultaneously test for INH and RIF resistance. This algorithm is feasible when mWRD testing can be conducted on-site or accessed through a reliable referral system with short turnaround times. The WHO operational handbook on TB diagnostics emphasizes the importance of transitioning from smear microscopy to mWRDs as the initial diagnostic test for all individuals with signs and symptoms of TB. This transition is essential to improve diagnostic sensitivity and enable simultaneous detection of RIF resistance (and INH resistance with moderate-complexity automated NAATs).
